front: The eight families of common tools
back: Expert judgment; data gathering; data analysis; data representation; decision-making; interpersonal and team skills; meetings; project management information system (PMIS).
Judgment based on expertise in an application area, discipline or industry, from any person or group with specialized knowledge, skill or experience.
The tools used to gather, integrate and distribute the outputs of project management processes: scheduling software, configuration management, reporting.

front: Data gathering vs data analysis vs data representation
back: Gathering: collect information. Analysis: make sense of it. Representation: show it.
A group generates many ideas in a short time, led by a facilitator, without judging them at first.
Prequalified stakeholders and experts in a guided, conversational discussion about their expectations and attitudes.
Written questions for collecting information quickly from many respondents. Best for large or geographically dispersed audiences.
Comparing products, processes and practices with those of comparable organizations to find best practices and ideas for improvement.
Evaluating the identified options to select the approach to use for the work.
Finding the basic underlying reason for a variance, defect or risk. Remove the root cause and the problem does not recur.
Determining the cause and degree of difference between the baseline and actual performance. Looks back.
Forecasting future outcomes from historical results. Looks forward and gives early warning.
Evaluating scenarios to predict their effect on project objectives.
Shows a large number of ideas classified into groups for review and analysis.
A diagram that organizes ideas visually around a topic, showing what they have in common and where they differ.
A visible, physical display placed where everyone can see it, updated frequently and often maintained by hand. Example: a task board.
Burndown: work remaining against time left in a timebox. Burnup: work completed toward a milestone.
A decision in which everyone agrees on a single course of action.
A decision supported by more than 50% of the group.
A decision in which the largest block decides, even if a majority is not achieved. Used when there are more than two options.
One individual makes the decision for the group.
A decision matrix: criteria are weighted, each alternative is scored, and the alternatives are ranked by score.
A prioritization method: must have, should have, could have, will not have.
Guiding a group event to a successful decision or conclusion, with effective participation and full buy-in.
Acknowledging, clarifying and confirming what is said, to reduce misunderstanding.
Getting cooperation from others without direct authority over them.
A structured method that collects each participant's input before discussion, so that vocal members do not dominate.
A brief daily meeting: progress since yesterday, intentions for today, obstacles. Also called a daily standup.
A regular workshop where the team explores how it worked in order to improve the process. Held at least at the end of each iteration.
Sprint review: show the completed product to stakeholders and get feedback. Retrospective: improve the team's process.
Distribute an agenda with objectives; invite the right people; start and finish on time; stay on topic; record actions and owners.
